provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation: Original mechanism: a single red cell and a single green cell are joined by an L-shaped path of cyan (8). The path leaves red along red's row until it reaches green's column. That corner cell is filled. It then runs along green's column to green. Endpoints are not recoloured, and only background cells are painted. Under D4, a horizontal flip keeps rows as rows, so the corner stays at (red row, green column). Each clockwise rotation swaps the row and column axes: original (r,c) becomes (c, H-1-r). For odd d4%4 the corner therefore lands at (green's visible row, red's visible column). Direction along each leg is not hard-coded. It is taken from the relative positions of the two visible cells, so reflections and reversals follow automatically. Colours are specialised as constants: background palette[0], red palette[2], green palette[3], fill palette[8]. The emitted program works directly in visible coordinates. It locates the two cells, picks the corner using the axis-swap flag, walks red to corner (corner included) and then corner to green (green excluded), and paints background cells with the fill colour.
draft_notes.limitations: Assumes exactly one red and one green cell, as the constructor guarantees. If either is missing, the input is returned unchanged; if there are several, the first in row-major order is used. The constructor samples distinct rows and distinct columns, so the L always has a real bend. The code still degrades sensibly to a straight segment if they were aligned. The archived solver's guard against overwriting non-background cells is kept, but it never triggers in the constructor's domain. No fixture contradictions or constructor defects were found. All three train pairs and the test pair agree with the corner at (red row, green column) in canonical orientation.

independent_source_review.mechanism: There is exactly one red cell and one green cell, in distinct rows and distinct columns, on a background. The output adds an L-shaped path of the fill colour. It runs from red along red's row to a corner at (red row, green column), corner included. It then runs along green's column to green, green excluded. Endpoints are never recoloured. In visible coordinates the corner becomes (green row, red column) whenever the D4 element swaps axes (odd quarter-turn component). Leg directions come from the relative positions of the visible cells.
evidence: Constructor `hpwl` places s=red at (rows[0],cols[0]) and e=green at (rows[1],cols[1]).
In `hpwl`, the horizontal loop `range(cols[0]+col_dir, cols[1], col_dir)` paints red's row up to but excluding green's column.

In `hpwl`, the vertical loop `range(rows[0], rows[1], row_dir)` paints green's column from red's row (the corner) up to but excluding green's row. The path is therefore red-exclusive, corner-inclusive and green-exclusive, which is what the factory emits: `_seg(rp, corner) + _seg(corner, gp)[:-1]`.
The red cell itself is never overwritten, because `range(rows[0], ...)` touches only column cols[1] and cols[0] != cols[1].

`common.sample(range(1,height-2),2)` and `common.sample(range(1,width-2),2)` give distinct rows and distinct columns. So corner != red, corner != green, and there are no degenerate straight segments or ties. `_seg`'s r-first stepping only ever handles single-axis segments in this domain.

Axis-swap logic is correct. Under rotation (r,c)->(c,H-1-r) or transpose, red's row becomes a visible column and green's column becomes a visible row, so the corner moves to (green visible row, red visible column). Horizontal and vertical flips keep the axes, so the corner stays at (red row, green column). `(d4%4)%2==1` selects exactly the axis-swapping elements under the rot^k∘flip encoding. The same `d4 % 2` axis convention appears in the supplied context checks.

The emitted solver locates cells and draws directly in visible coordinates. It has no whole-grid untransform/retransform wrapper. CORNER_GREEN_ROW_RED_COL is a genuine orientation constant, and every demonstration under a given augmentation shows it consistently.

Colours are taken from the palette as constants: palette[0], palette[2], palette[3] and palette[8]. These are the real rule colours, visible in every demonstration. There is no arbitrary colour lookup needing extra evidence.

All four fixtures match the constructor's validate() parameters with red=(rows[0],cols[0]). For the test, red is at (2,1) and green at (10,10): row 2 cols 2..10 and column 10 rows 3..9 are painted, which matches the fixture.
The archived program is equivalent: row ry from rx+step through gx inclusive, then column gx from ry+step to gy exclusive.
The host audit passed 1000 fresh pairs and 8000 augmented checks with no sampler rejections. This is consistent with the source review but was not relied on as proof.
nonblocking_limits: Behaviour with missing or duplicate red/green cells (returns the grid unchanged, or uses the first cell in row-major order) is an out-of-domain fallback. The constructor always places exactly one of each.
The BG-only paint guard and aligned-endpoint degradation never trigger in the constructor domain, since rows and columns are always distinct and there are no other objects.

Correctness of the axis-swap flag assumes the host's D4 index encoding puts axis-swapping elements at odd d4%4. This is consistent with the supplied context-check convention and with the host's augmented pass, but the encoding itself was not shown in source.
required_context_checks: Standard D4 conflicting-answer rejection only. The corner orientation is shown consistently by every demonstration, and no colour-association evidence check is needed.

draft_notes.host_review: Reviewed mechanism and limitations. Confirmed augmentation.py uses a bijective palette, horizontal flip followed by clockwise turns; audit.py checks every D4, not only its final reported d4=7. Episode-wide D4 ambiguity gate is active. Out-of-domain fallbacks do not justify unverified inputs; every export still executes the program on every pair.
